terms.def: The dominant HVAC refrigeration method: compressor → condenser → expansion device → evaporator. Transfers heat from low to high temperature using work input.
Dimensionless ratio of desired heat output (or cooling effect) to compressor work input. Can exceed 1 because heat is pumped, not generated.
Reversible adiabatic process — entropy is constant (s₁ = s₂). Models ideal compressor compression.
Constant-enthalpy process (h₃ = h₄). Models adiabatic expansion across the expansion device.
Refrigerant temperature above its saturation temperature at the current pressure. 10–20°F at compressor inlet prevents liquid slugging.
Liquid refrigerant cooled ~15°F below condensing saturation temperature. Ensures 100% liquid at expansion device and increases system capacity.
Energy Efficiency Ratio (Btu/W·h). COP = EER / 3.412. Higher EER = more efficient.
Ozone Depletion Potential (relative to R-11); Global Warming Potential (relative to CO₂). CFCs: high ODP. HFCs: ODP=0 but high GWP.

learn.title: 1 · The Vapor Compression Cycle
learn.body:
The purpose of a refrigeration cycle is to transfer heat from a region of low temperature to a region of higher temperature. The dominant method in HVAC is the single-stage vapor compression cycle (VCC). The cycle has four processes and four key state points:

  • Point 1→2 (Compressor): Low-pressure gas is compressed to high pressure and temperature. Ideally isentropic (s₁ = s₂).
  • Point 2→3 (Condenser): Superheated vapor is cooled then condensed to saturated liquid at constant pressure. Heat is rejected to the environment.
  • Point 3→4 (Expansion Device): High-pressure liquid drops to low pressure at constant enthalpy (h₃ = h₄). Refrigerant partially flashes to vapor.
  • Point 4→1 (Evaporator): Low-pressure mixture evaporates at constant pressure, absorbing heat from the cooled space.

Because heat is "pumped," the system delivers more heat to the condenser than the work input — which is why COP can exceed 1.

learn.title: 2 · COP and Carnot Efficiency
learn.body:
The Coefficient of Performance (COP) is the ratio of desired output to work input. For the ideal Carnot cycle:

COP_cooling = T_evap / (T_cond − T_evap)   [absolute °R or K]
COP_heating  = T_cond / (T_cond − T_evap)
COP_heating = COP_cooling + 1   (always)

For real cycles using p-h diagram enthalpy values:

COP_c = (h₁ − h₄) / (h₂ − h₁)
COP_h = (h₂ − h₃) / (h₂ − h₁)

Real COP is always less than Carnot due to irreversibilities. In US practice: COP = EER / 3.412 and for chillers: COP = 3.52 / (kW/ton).

learn.title: 3 · Thermodynamic Properties & the p-h Diagram
learn.body:
Key properties: Enthalpy (h) = u + pv (Btu/lb) — total energy tracked at each cycle point. Entropy (s) — irreversible processes generate it. Saturation temperature — temperature at which phase change occurs at a given pressure; high-side = condensing temperature t_c, low-side = evaporating temperature t_e.

The pressure-enthalpy (p-h) diagram has enthalpy on the x-axis, pressure on y-axis. The dome-shaped curve separates: left of dome = subcooled liquid; under dome = two-phase mixture; right of dome = superheated vapor.

A superheat of 10–20°F at compressor inlet protects against liquid slugging. Subcooling of ~15°F at the condenser outlet ensures 100% liquid enters the expansion device and increases system capacity.

learn.title: 4 · Real Cycle Irreversibilities
learn.body:
The second law of thermodynamics governs real system behavior. Every real process generates entropy, reducing efficiency below the Carnot ideal. Key irreversibilities in a real VCC:

  • Superheated inlet gas → lower density → reduced mass flow → reduced capacity
  • Pressure drops across valves, ports, mufflers → more work required
  • Condenser operates at temperatures above the ideal condensing temperature
  • Evaporator operates at temperatures below the ideal evaporating temperature
  • Zeotropic refrigerant blends exhibit temperature glide during phase change → lower efficiency

An isentropic process has constant entropy (s₁ = s₂). An adiabatic expansion across the expansion valve is modeled as isenthalpic (h₃ = h₄) — not isentropic because entropy increases.

learn.title: 5 · Refrigerants: Types, Numbering & Environment
learn.body:
The refrigerant numbering formula for methane/ethane/propane derivatives:

R-[C−1][H+1][F]   e.g. R-22 = CHClF₂ → R-022

Refrigerant families: CFCs (R-1xx, R-5xx) — high ozone depletion; phased out by 1996 Montreal Protocol. HCFCs (R-22) — lower ODP (0.034); phase-out ~2020. HFCs (R-134a, R-410a, R-407c) — zero ODP; still have GWP concerns.

Environmental metrics: ODP (Ozone Depletion Potential, relative to R-11). GWP (Global Warming Potential, relative to CO₂). TEWI — Total Equivalent Warming Impact, combines GWP + energy consumption effect.

ASHRAE Standard 34 safety classification: letter = toxicity (A = low, B = toxic); number = flammability (1 = none, 2 = low, 3 = high). e.g. R-134a = A1.

learn.title: 6 · Expansion Devices & Compressor Types
learn.body:
Expansion Devices: TXV (Thermostatic Expansion Valve) — senses suction superheat via a bulb; rising superheat opens valve for more flow; self-regulating. Capillary tube — fixed length/diameter; simple but cannot modulate; used in small units. Short-tube restrictor — compact version; can act as check valve in heat pump. Four-way reversing valve — routes refrigerant to switch heat pump between heating and cooling modes.

Compressor Types: Hermetic reciprocating — motor + compressor sealed; common small-to-medium. Hermetic scroll — orbiting scroll; fewer moving parts, slightly higher efficiency. Rotary vane — medium applications. Twin-screw (open drive) — larger commercial. Centrifugal — large commercial chillers; highest capacity.

reading.title: HVAC Simplified — Chapter 2: HVAC Fundamentals: Refrigeration
reading.source: Kavanaugh, S.P. (2006). HVAC Simplified. ASHRAE Press. Chapter 2, pp. 5–18.

paragraphs.text: The purpose of a refrigeration cycle is to transfer heat from a region of low temperature to a region of higher temperature. There is a variety of thermodynamic cycles for this purpose, but discussion in this section is limited to the single-stage vapor compression cycle, which is the dominant method used in air-conditioning (cooling-only) units and heat pumps (heating and cooling). The heart of the cycle is the compressor, which elevates the pressure and temperature of a refrigerant gas. At the elevated temperature, heat is rejected to the environment (cooling mode) or to the indoor space (heating mode). After the refrigerant has released heat, it is a liquid at high pressure and flows to an expansion device. This device reduces the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant, which initiates evaporation of the liquid at low temperature. At this temperature, heat is removed from the indoor space (cooling mode) or the environment (heating mode). The refrigerant gas then enters the compressor to repeat the cycle.

Refrigerant enters the compressor as a low-temperature and low-pressure gas (point 1). Work (W) is required to drive the compressor so it can elevate the refrigerant to a higher pressure and temperature. The refrigerant exits the compressor as a superheated vapor (point 2) and enters the condenser. At the higher temperature, heat is rejected to the environment through a condenser (heat exchanger), which lowers the temperature of the refrigerant vapor and then converts it to a liquid. The warm liquid refrigerant exits the condenser (point 3) and enters the expansion device. As the refrigerant leaves the expansion device (point 4), its pressure is now lower than the saturation pressure of the surrounding fluid so it begins to flash in the evaporator. The cooling effect is accomplished in the evaporator as the fluid (typically air or water) is passed through the opposite side of this heat exchanger and its temperature is reduced by the evaporating refrigerant. The refrigerant exits the evaporator as low-temperature and low-pressure gas to complete the cycle at point 1.

This process is referred to as the Carnot refrigeration cycle. It is an attractive thermodynamic process because heat is being 'pumped' from one level (temperature) to another. Therefore, it is possible to deliver heat at a rate greater than the required input power. This provides an advantage over heating processes that convert heat from chemical or electrical energy that cannot exceed conversion efficiencies of 100%.

The efficiency, or dimensionless coefficient of performance (COP), of a Carnot refrigeration cycle is limited by the temperature of the heat source (evaporating temperature, te) and the heat sink (condensing temperature, tc). If cooling is the intended effect of the cycle, the theoretical COP is: COP_c = te / (tc − te), where temperatures are in absolute units (°R or K). If the intended effect is heating (heat pump in heating mode), the theoretical COP is: COP_h = tc / (tc − te). The COP values generated with these equations assume the process is completely reversible. However, the second law of thermodynamics is used to describe the irreversibilities in real processes due to pressure drops, mechanical friction, heat transfer, etc., in terms of entropy flow.

For real cycles, the COP is computed from p-h diagram enthalpy values rather than Carnot temperatures. For cooling: COP_c = (h1 − h4) / (h2 − h1). For heating: COP_h = (h2 − h3) / (h2 − h1). Note that COP_h = COP_c + 1 always holds. It should be noted that the values computed for COP_c and COP_h using real-cycle enthalpy values are idealized theoretical values for a specific refrigerant and should always be less than the corresponding Carnot values. In US practice, COP relates to EER as: COP = EER / 3.412. For chillers: COP = 3.52 / (kW/ton).

An important concept to remember in these systems is the relationship between the pressure of the refrigerant and the saturation temperature at that point. The high-pressure side of the system (compressor discharge to expansion device inlet) operates at a relatively constant pressure. The corresponding saturation temperature is referred to as the condensing temperature (tc). The refrigerant enters the condenser above this temperature, but once it has been desuperheated and begins to condense, the temperature will be essentially constant until it is 100% liquid. In an ideal system the refrigerant will exit the condenser at this state, but in a real system it is typically subcooled several degrees before entering the expansion device.

On the low-pressure side of the system (expansion device outlet to compressor inlet), the saturation temperature is referred to as the evaporating temperature (te). The refrigerant typically enters the evaporator at this temperature and remains relatively constant until it is 100% vapor. In a real system it is typically superheated several degrees before entering the compressor inlet (suction). Both ideal and real vapor compression cycles can be analyzed with pressure-enthalpy (p-h) diagrams. In this case, enthalpy is used to quantify the energy of the refrigerant per unit mass at various points in the cycle. The dome-shaped curve separates: left of dome = subcooled liquid; under dome = two-phase mixture (quality 0–1); right of dome = superheated vapor. Superheat of 10–20°F at the compressor inlet protects against liquid slugging. Subcooling of approximately 15°F at the condenser outlet ensures 100% liquid enters the expansion device and increases system capacity.

A familiarity with the ideal cycle process is valuable even though it is idealized. Limits are set and the system designer can determine the relative importance of operating conditions and component selection that will have the greatest impact on total system optimization. However, there are a number of constraints that limit the capacity and efficiency of actual vapor compression cycles. Refrigerant enters the compressor as a superheated vapor to protect it from damage by liquid refrigerant (liquid is essentially incompressible and may damage the compressor). Superheated gas has a lower density (higher specific volume) than saturated vapor; therefore, the compressor handles less mass flow per unit of displacement volume, reducing system capacity.

Pressure drops occur across heat exchangers (condenser and evaporator), valves, ports, and mufflers, requiring additional compressor work. The condenser must operate at a temperature above the temperature of the heat sink to which it is rejecting heat; the evaporator must operate at a temperature below the temperature of the medium being cooled. These real-world temperature differences represent irreversibilities that reduce the COP below the Carnot ideal. Zeotropic refrigerant blends (mixtures) exhibit temperature glide during phase change — the temperature at which the blend evaporates or condenses changes as the composition of the vapor and liquid phases shift — which further reduces cycle efficiency compared to pure refrigerants.

Refrigerants are numbered according to the chemical formula. For methane, ethane, and propane derivatives the numbering follows: R-[C−1][H+1][F], where C = number of carbon atoms, H = hydrogen atoms, F = fluorine atoms. For example, R-22 (CHClF2): [1−1][1+1][2] = R-022. Refrigerant families and environmental impact: CFCs (R-11, R-12, R-113, R-114, R-500, R-502) — fully halogenated; high ozone depletion potential (ODP); phased out under the Montreal Protocol by 1996. HCFCs (R-22, R-123) — partially halogenated; lower ODP (~0.034 for R-22); phase-out target approximately 2020. HFCs (R-134a, R-410A, R-407C) — no chlorine; ODP = 0; but have significant global warming potential (GWP).

Environmental metrics: Ozone Depletion Potential (ODP) is measured relative to R-11 (ODP = 1.0). Global Warming Potential (GWP) is measured relative to CO2 (GWP = 1). Total Equivalent Warming Impact (TEWI) combines the direct GWP of refrigerant emissions with the indirect greenhouse gas emissions from the energy consumed to run the system over its lifetime — it is a more complete measure of environmental impact than GWP alone. ASHRAE Standard 34 classifies refrigerants by a letter-number code: letter indicates toxicity (A = low, B = higher toxicity); number indicates flammability (1 = no flame propagation, 2L = low flammability, 2 = flammable, 3 = highly flammable). For example, R-134a is classified A1 (low toxicity, non-flammable).

Thermostatic expansion valves (TXVs) are the most widely used modulating expansion devices. A sensing bulb is strapped to the suction line near the compressor inlet and detects the refrigerant's suction superheat. When superheat increases above the set point, the higher bulb pressure acts on a diaphragm, forcing the valve stem open to allow more refrigerant to flow. As more refrigerant flows, the superheat decreases back to the set point. This self-regulating behavior makes the TXV effective across a wide range of operating conditions. Capillary tubes are fixed-length, fixed-diameter tubes used as expansion devices in small systems (window ACs, residential refrigerators). They are simple and inexpensive but cannot modulate flow in response to changing conditions. Short-tube restrictors are similar to capillary tubes but shorter; they can also act as check valves in heat pump reversing applications.

Compressor types used in HVAC applications: Hermetic reciprocating — motor and compressor are sealed in a common housing; piston-and-cylinder design; widely used in small-to-medium residential and commercial equipment. Hermetic scroll — an orbiting scroll wraps against a fixed scroll to progressively compress refrigerant gas; fewer moving parts than reciprocating; somewhat quieter and slightly more efficient; now dominant in residential split systems. Rotary vane — a rotor with sliding vanes rotates inside a cylinder; medium-size applications. Twin-screw (open drive) — intermeshing helical rotors; used in larger commercial chillers and industrial refrigeration. Centrifugal — a high-speed impeller accelerates refrigerant gas; used in large commercial chillers handling hundreds of tons of refrigeration; highest capacity of any compressor type. The choice of compressor affects system efficiency (EER), noise, maintenance requirements, and the range of operating conditions over which the system can reliably operate. (See also: practicalhvac.com for component animations and descriptions.)

anki.q: What is the purpose of a refrigeration cycle?
anki.a: To transfer heat from a region of low temperature to a region of higher temperature, using work input.

anki.q: Name the four processes of the ideal vapor compression cycle in order.
anki.a: 1→2: Isentropic compression · 2→3: Constant-pressure condensation · 3→4: Isenthalpic expansion · 4→1: Constant-pressure evaporation.

anki.q: What is the condition at the compressor inlet (Point 1) in the ideal VCC?
anki.a: Saturated vapor at the evaporating temperature and pressure (low side).

anki.q: What happens in the condenser (Point 2→3)?
anki.a: Superheated vapor is desuperheated, then condensed to saturated liquid at constant pressure. Heat is rejected to the environment.

anki.q: What is the thermodynamic relationship across the expansion device? Why?
anki.a: h₃ = h₄ (isenthalpic). The expansion is adiabatic with no work done, so enthalpy is conserved.

anki.q: Why can COP of a refrigeration cycle exceed 1?
anki.a: Heat is pumped rather than generated. The cycle moves existing thermal energy, so the delivered heat or cooling effect can exceed the compressor work input.

anki.q: Write the Carnot COP formula for a cooling cycle.
anki.a: COP_c = T_e / (T_c − T_e) — temperatures must be in absolute units (°R or K).

anki.q: Write the Carnot COP formula for a heating (heat pump) cycle.
anki.a: COP_h = T_c / (T_c − T_e). Always: COP_h = COP_c + 1.

anki.q: Write the real-cycle COP_cooling using enthalpy.
anki.a: COP_c = (h₁ − h₄) / (h₂ − h₁) = cooling effect ÷ compressor work.

anki.q: How do you convert EER (Btu/W·h) to COP?
anki.a: COP = EER / 3.412.

anki.q: How do you convert kW/ton to COP?
anki.a: COP = 3.52 / (kW/ton). A ton = 12,000 Btu/h.

anki.q: How is 1 ton of refrigeration defined?
anki.a: The rate of heat removal needed to convert 2000 lb of water at 32°F to ice at 32°F in 24 hours = 12,000 Btu/h.

anki.q: Define enthalpy (h).
anki.a: h = u + pv. Sum of internal energy and pressure × volume work. Units: Btu/lb.

anki.q: Define entropy (s).
anki.a: Ratio of heat absorbed by a substance to the absolute temperature at which it was added. Irreversible processes generate entropy.

anki.q: What is an isentropic process?
anki.a: A reversible adiabatic process — entropy is constant (s₁ = s₂). Ideal compressor compression is isentropic.

anki.q: What is an adiabatic process?
anki.a: A process where no heat is exchanged with the surroundings. Note: adiabatic ≠ isentropic unless also reversible.

anki.q: What is the condensing temperature (t_c)?
anki.a: The saturation temperature on the high-pressure side — the temperature at which the refrigerant condenses at the condenser operating pressure.

anki.q: What is the evaporating temperature (t_e)?
anki.a: The saturation temperature on the low-pressure side — the temperature at which refrigerant evaporates at the evaporator operating pressure.

anki.q: What is superheat in a refrigerant system?
anki.a: Temperature of the refrigerant above its saturation temperature at the current pressure. Measured at the compressor inlet; protects against liquid slugging.

anki.q: What is subcooling? Why is it used?
anki.a: Cooling the liquid refrigerant ~15°F below its saturation temperature at condenser pressure. Ensures 100% liquid enters expansion device and increases system capacity.

anki.q: On a p-h diagram, what do the left and right sides of the saturation dome represent?
anki.a: Left = saturated liquid line · Right = saturated vapor line · Under dome = two-phase mixture · Right of dome = superheated vapor · Left of dome = subcooled liquid.

anki.q: On a p-h diagram, the isentropic compression line runs in which direction?
anki.a: Vertically up-and-to-the-right — constant entropy line (isentrope) from low-pressure saturated vapor into the superheated vapor region.

anki.q: Name three sources of irreversibility in a real vapor compression cycle.
anki.a: 1) Pressure drops across valves/ports · 2) Heat generation from friction · 3) Finite heat exchangers (condenser runs hotter than ideal; evaporator runs colder than ideal).

anki.q: Why does superheated inlet gas reduce compressor capacity?
anki.a: Superheated gas has lower density (higher specific volume) → lower mass flow rate per unit displacement → reduced refrigeration capacity.

anki.q: What is the refrigerant numbering formula for methane/ethane/propane derivatives?
What are the three CFC/HCFC/HFC families and their key environmental difference?
anki.a: CFCs: High ODP, phased out 1996 · HCFCs: Lower ODP (R-22 ODP=0.034), phase-out ~2020 · HFCs: Zero ODP but high GWP (R-134a, R-410a).

anki.q: What does ODP stand for and what is it relative to?
anki.a: Ozone Depletion Potential. Relative to R-11 (CCl₃F = 1.0). HFCs have ODP = 0.

anki.q: What is TEWI?
anki.a: Total Equivalent Warming Impact — combines the refrigerant's direct GWP with the indirect greenhouse gas emissions from the energy needed to run the system.

anki.q: What does ASHRAE Standard 34 safety class 'A2' mean?
anki.a: A = low chronic toxicity · 2 = low flammability (low LFL and heat of combustion < 8174 Btu/lb).

anki.q: How does a TXV (thermostatic expansion valve) control refrigerant flow?
anki.a: A sensing bulb on the suction line detects superheat. Rising superheat → higher bulb pressure → diaphragm opens valve → more refrigerant flow → superheat drops back to set point.

anki.q: What is the advantage of a scroll compressor over a reciprocating compressor?
anki.a: Fewer moving parts, smoother operation, and slightly higher efficiency due to reduced friction and pressure losses.

anki.q: What does a four-way reversing valve do in a heat pump?
anki.a: It reverses the refrigerant flow direction to switch between heating and cooling modes, swapping the roles of the indoor and outdoor coils as condenser/evaporator.

quiz.q: In the ideal VCC, what is the thermodynamic process across the expansion device?
quiz.explanation: h₃ = h₄. The expansion is adiabatic with no work output, so enthalpy is conserved. It is not isentropic because entropy increases (irreversible).

quiz.q: A system has T_evap = 40°F (500°R) and T_cond = 120°F (580°R). What is the Carnot COP for cooling?
What does a higher EER value indicate?
quiz.explanation: EER = capacity (Btu/h) / power (W). Higher EER = more cooling per watt of electricity consumed = more efficient.

quiz.q: Which refrigerant property is constant along the lines inside the saturation dome on a p-h diagram?
quiz.explanation: Inside the two-phase dome, temperature and pressure are coupled (saturation condition) — both remain constant as quality changes.

quiz.q: R-22 has an ODP of 0.034. What does this mean for ozone depletion compared to R-11?
options: Causes 3.4% of the ozone depletion of R-11
quiz.explanation: ODP is relative to R-11 = 1.0. ODP of 0.034 means R-22 causes 3.4% of the ozone destruction that R-11 would.

quiz.q: In a real VCC, a compressor with superheated suction gas will have _______ compared to saturated vapor inlet.
options: Higher mass flow rate, higher capacity
Lower mass flow rate, lower capacity
Same mass flow rate, lower efficiency
quiz.explanation: Superheated gas has lower density → compressor moves less mass per revolution → lower refrigerant mass flow → lower cooling capacity.

quiz.q: What is the definition of 1 ton of refrigeration?
quiz.explanation: 1 ton = 12,000 Btu/h. It equals the rate needed to freeze 1 ton (2000 lb) of water at 32°F in 24 hours.

quiz.q: Which component in a heat pump system allows switching between heating and cooling modes?
quiz.explanation: The four-way reversing valve routes refrigerant so the indoor coil acts as condenser (heating) or evaporator (cooling).

quiz.q: What ASHRAE Standard 34 safety classification does R-134a belong to?
options: A1 — low toxicity, no flame propagation
quiz.explanation: R-134a is classified A1: A = no identifiable chronic toxicity; 1 = no flame propagation in standard air.

quiz.q: For R-22, using the numbering rule R-[C−1][H+1][F], CHClF₂ gives:
quiz.explanation: Carbon=1→C−1=0; Hydrogen=1→H+1=2; Fluorine=2. Result: R-022 = R-22.

quiz.q: Subcooling the liquid refrigerant 15°F below the condensing temperature:
options: Increases system capacity and ensures 100% liquid at expansion device
Has no effect on cycle performance
quiz.explanation: Subcooling lowers liquid enthalpy (h₃), allowing more heat absorption in the evaporator and preventing flash gas at the expansion device.

quiz.q: In the p-h cycle diagram, which leg represents the compressor work input?
quiz.explanation: w_comp = h₂ − h₁. The compressor raises enthalpy from low-side saturated vapor (h₁) to high-side superheated vapor (h₂).
